summary: This document creates the SIP Resource Priority header namespace esnet and registers it with IANA. The namespace allows local emergency sessions to be set up to a public safety answering point (PSAP), between PSAPs, and between a PSAP and first responders.

eli5.summary: Emergency calls sometimes need to skip the line. This creates a special pass name for local emergency call centers and first responders.

questions: how do emergency calls get priority
sip resource priority for emergency services
subtitle: Priority labels for emergency calls in controlled networks

tldr.problem: Emergency call centers and first responders need a way to mark their calls for priority handling within controlled IP networks, distinguishing them from regular calls.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7135 creates the 'esnet' namespace for the SIP Resource Priority header, which allows emergency sessions to request preferential treatment with one of five priority levels (0 through 4).
tldr.outcome: Emergency services can now give their calls priority treatment within emergency services networks and IP Multimedia Subsystems, where abuse can be controlled through network management.

facts.label: Intended use
facts.value: Emergency services networks and IP Multimedia Subsystems only

today: RFC 7135 is an Informational specification that has not been obsoleted. It remains the definition of the 'esnet' SIP Resource Priority namespace for emergency communications within controlled networks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) is used to set up voice and video calls over IP networks. RFC 7135 defines a new way to mark emergency calls for priority treatment by creating the 'esnet' namespace for the SIP Resource Priority header. The RFC itself does not define how networks should treat these priority calls, but it registers the namespace so emergency systems can use it consistently.

The 'esnet' namespace is designed specifically for use within controlled networks like Emergency Services Networks (ESInets) and IP Multimedia Subsystems, where administrators can enforce policies and prevent misuse. It is not intended for use on the open public Internet because the header can be easily forged.
sections.eli5: In an emergency network, important calls need special treatment. This creates a label that says 'this is an emergency call, please prioritize it.'

sections.title: Where and How the Namespace is Used
sections.content:
The 'esnet' namespace has specific rules about when it should be used. It MUST only be used when at least one end of the call is within a local emergency organization—either the caller or the receiver (or someone in between) must be an emergency service provider or first responder. This includes calls to a PSAP (Public Safety Answering Point, the 911-equivalent center), calls between PSAPs, and calls from a PSAP to first responders.

Unlike a simple marking that just identifies an emergency call, the Resource Priority header specifically requests preferential network treatment. Both can be used together: the emergency identifier marks what the call is for, while the Resource Priority namespace requests the network to allocate resources accordingly.
sections.eli5: The priority label can only be used when a real emergency organization is involved in the call. It tells the network, 'please treat this call better than normal calls.'

sections.title: The esnet Namespace and Its Priority Levels
sections.content:
The 'esnet' namespace provides five priority levels, numbered 0 (lowest) through 4 (highest): esnet.0, esnet.1, esnet.2, esnet.3, and esnet.4. This allows emergency systems to differentiate between different types of emergency calls according to their local policies. For example, a call from an ordinary citizen to a PSAP might receive priority level 1, while a call from one PSAP to another or from a PSAP to the national emergency management might receive level 4.

The RFC does not prescribe which types of calls should use which priority levels—that is left to each jurisdiction or emergency network to define through local policy. The namespace is registered as a queue-based system, which means calls are placed in priority queues, but preemption (disconnecting a lower-priority call to make room for higher) is optional and requires explicit configuration.
sections.eli5: The 'esnet' system gives emergency calls a number from 0 to 4, with 4 being the most important. Each area can decide which types of calls get which numbers based on their needs.

sections.title: How the Namespace Fits into Emergency Networks
sections.content:
RFC 7135 includes a network diagram showing how the 'esnet' namespace is used. Emergency calls originating from regular user networks flow through proxies to the emergency services network (ESInet), where the 'esnet' namespace can be used. Inside the ESInet, all calls between PSAPs and to first responders (police, fire, national agencies) can use the priority marking. Application Service Providers that connect securely to the ESInet may also be allowed to use the namespace if there is a trust relationship with the emergency network.

The namespace may also be used for calls going outbound from the ESInet back to the general network when callback or follow-up communication is needed. The exact handling of priority at the boundaries between the public network and the ESInet is left to local administration.
sections.eli5: Emergency networks have special boundaries where calls come in and go out. The priority label can be used inside the emergency network and by trusted partners connected to it.

sections.title: Security and Scope Limitations
sections.content:
The main security concern is that the SIP Resource Priority header is easy to forge on open networks. An attacker could attach the 'esnet' label to a regular call to trick networks into giving it priority. This is why RFC 7135 explicitly limits 'esnet' to use within managed networks like ESInets and IP Multimedia Subsystems, where administrators can monitor and control who is allowed to set these headers.

The RFC clarifies that precautions must be taken to prevent unauthorized users from marking their calls as 'esnet' priority. One simple approach is to not honor 'esnet' priority markings unless the destination is known to be part of the local emergency system. The rules from RFC 4412 (the base Resource Priority specification) apply to everything else about how the header behaves.
sections.eli5: Anyone could write a fake priority label on their own messages. To stay safe, emergency networks only trust these labels when they come through special, protected connections.
